subChunks.title: Threads & the Thread Lifecycle

storyBeats.text: Eldrin summons three apprentice golems simultaneously — each begins a separate task at the same instant. The spell chamber echoes with three different incantations being cast in parallel.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: A thread is a parallel stream of execution. Your program's main method runs on the main thread. Every new Thread you create and start() runs concurrently. Note: start(), not run(). Calling run() directly does not start a new thread.

storyBeats.label: Two threads

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: join() is the waiting ward — it blocks the current thread until the target thread finishes. Without it, your main method might exit before your worker threads complete their work.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Create two threads using lambda Runnables. Thread 1 prints "T1: 0" through "T1: 2". Thread 2 prints "T2: 0" through "T2: 2". Start both and join both so the main thread waits for completion.
guidedPractice.hint: Use new Thread(() -> { ... }) for each. Call t1.start(); t2.start(); t1.join(); t2.join(); then print Done.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the Thread lifecycle in Java. What is the difference between calling start() and run() on a Thread?

questions.prompt: What is the correct way to start a new thread of execution in Java?
questions.explanation: start() creates a new OS thread and calls run() inside it. Calling run() directly executes on the current thread — no new thread is created.

questions.prompt: The order in which threads print output is always the same between runs.
questions.explanation: Thread scheduling is non-deterministic. The OS decides which thread runs when — output order can vary between runs, which is exactly why concurrent programming is challenging.

subChunks.title: Synchronisation & Race Conditions

storyBeats.text: Two golems simultaneously reach for the same mana crystal, each trying to record how much power they've drawn. Their simultaneous reads and writes collide — the total is wrong.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: That is a race condition. The golems compete for a shared resource without coordination. synchronized places a ward around the critical section — only one golem may enter at a time. The others wait.

storyBeats.label: Synchronized counter

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: AtomicInteger uses CPU-level compare-and-swap operations — faster than a synchronized lock for a single counter. For more complex invariants spanning multiple variables, synchronized is still necessary.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Create an AtomicInteger counter. Start 10 threads, each incrementing it 100 times. After joining all threads, print the final count (should always be 1000).
guidedPractice.hint: Use AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() inside each thread. Join all threads before printing.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: What is a race condition? Explain how synchronized and AtomicInteger each prevent data corruption in multi-threaded code.

options: Only one thread executes the synchronized code at a time
All threads run at the same speed
questions.answer: Only one thread executes the synchronized code at a time
questions.explanation: synchronized acquires the object's intrinsic lock. Other threads attempting to enter a synchronized method/block on the same object block until the lock is released.

options: n++ is not atomic — read, increment, write can interleave between threads losing updates
questions.answer: n++ is not atomic — read, increment, write can interleave between threads losing updates
questions.explanation: n++ is three operations (read, add, write). Two threads can both read the same value, both increment, and both write back — losing one update. Use synchronized or AtomicInteger.

subChunks.title: volatile, ThreadLocal & Deadlock

storyBeats.text: Two golems carry treasure — Golem A holds the gold key and wants the silver key; Golem B holds the silver key and wants the gold key. They stare at each other forever.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Deadlock is the eternal standoff. Neither thread can proceed because each holds what the other needs. Prevention is simple in principle: always acquire multiple locks in a consistent order. In practice, it requires discipline.

storyBeats.label: ThreadLocal example

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: ThreadLocal gives each thread its own isolated copy of a variable — a per-thread rune that no other thread can read or write. Used extensively in frameworks to carry request-scoped context like user sessions.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Demonstrate ThreadLocal: create a ThreadLocal<String>, set it to "Thread-A" in one thread and "Thread-B" in another. Each thread prints its own value. Both values should appear (order may vary).
guidedPractice.hint: Each thread calls local.set(...) then System.out.println(local.get()). ThreadLocal values are isolated per thread.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: What is the difference between volatile and synchronized? Explain what a deadlock is and how to prevent it.

options: Reads and writes go directly to main memory (visibility), not CPU caches
Only one thread can write the variable at a time (atomicity)
The variable is initialised to zero
questions.answer: Reads and writes go directly to main memory (visibility), not CPU caches
questions.explanation: volatile guarantees visibility — threads always see the latest value. It does NOT guarantee atomicity — compound operations like n++ still need synchronisation.

questions.prompt: ThreadLocal variables are shared between all threads that access them.
questions.explanation: ThreadLocal gives each thread its own independent copy of the variable. One thread's value cannot be seen by another thread — that is the entire purpose of ThreadLocal.
